title: Attack and defend: DNS tunneling
blurb: Learn how attackers hide data in DNS queries, recognize the pattern, and block it with Umbrella.
scenario: A workstation sends thousands of DNS queries an hour, all to subdomains of one unfamiliar domain. Nothing else about the host looks wrong. Work out what's going on, and make sure DNS can't be used as a covert channel.
topology: Workstation ── internal DNS ── Umbrella ── attacker's authoritative DNS server
objectives: Understand why DNS works as a covert channel
Configure Umbrella and the firewall to stop it

steps.title: Why DNS?
steps.learn: Almost every network lets DNS out, and DNS queries are **forwarded** across resolvers to whichever server is authoritative for a domain. An attacker who owns a domain can encode data in subdomain labels and read it on their own name server. Replies carry data back the other way.
steps.question: Why does DNS tunneling often get past firewalls?

options.text: DNS is allowed almost everywhere, and the traffic travels through legitimate resolvers to the attacker's name server, so it looks like normal lookups.
DNS traffic is encrypted, so firewalls can't read it.
options.why: Classic DNS is plain text. The problem is that it's trusted and rarely inspected.

options.text: DNS uses a random port each time.
options.why: DNS uses port 53. It's allowed, not hidden.

steps.title: Spot the pattern
steps.task: Pick every sign of tunneling in this query log.
steps.question:
`a9f3c1e07b2d4c88e1f0.d41b77.data-sync-cdn.net  TXT`
`0c7e19aa53f2be6d9c04.d41b78.data-sync-cdn.net  TXT`
`f1e2d3c4b5a69788a0b1.d41b79.data-sync-cdn.net  TXT`
(about 3,000 per hour, from one host)

options.text: A huge volume of unique queries to a single domain
Mostly TXT queries, which can carry larger answers

options.why: The top-level domain alone means nothing.

steps.title: Block it in Umbrella
steps.learn: Umbrella spots tunneling with models that look at entropy, volume and known tunneling tools, and offers it as a security category. Newly seen domains are another strong signal, because tunneling domains are usually registered just before use.
steps.task: In the HQ DNS policy, block **DNS Tunneling VPN**, **Newly Seen Domains** and **Command and Control Callbacks**.
steps.screen: Umbrella › Policies › DNS Policies › HQ-Policy › Security Settings

steps.title: Close the side doors
steps.task: Pick every control that stops the host from simply bypassing Umbrella.
steps.question: Which controls stop a host going around the protected resolver?

options.text: Block outbound UDP and TCP 53 from everything except the internal DNS servers.
Block or control DNS over HTTPS (DoH) to public resolvers, for example with the firewall's DoH application filter.
Allow port 53 to any address so troubleshooting is easier.
options.why: That lets any host query an outside resolver directly, around Umbrella.

summary: DNS as a trusted channel that reaches the attacker's name server, high-entropy labels, volume and TXT records as indicators, Umbrella's tunneling, newly seen and CnC categories, and locking down port 53 and DoH.
